backTranslations.41:
**Before the visit**
- Add your appointment date in the Visit tab. MenoMap shows how ready your summary is and what would strengthen it.
- Choose the topics and questions most important to you. Three or four is best.
- Prepare the summary for the last 30 or 90 days. Check that your medication list is up to date.

**At the visit**
- Hand over or show the first page. It's built to be read in under a minute: numbers, averages, the heat map and your questions.
- Start with the question most important to you.
- If your doctor speaks another language, you can produce the summary in that language.

**What the summary is, and what it is not**

It is a summary of what you entered, and of anything you chose to import from Health. It is not a diagnosis and not a full medical record, and any pattern shown in it is a coincidence check, not proof of cause. The doctor may ask questions the summary cannot answer, and that's normal.

**After the visit**

Add any new medication with its start date. In a few weeks MenoMap can show your records before and after, which will make the next follow-up appointment easier.
backTranslations.42:
**Menopause** is a single point in time: the day 12 consecutive months without a period were completed, when there is no other explanation (such as pregnancy, certain medications or surgery). In many countries it happens on average in the early 50s, but any age from the mid-40s to mid-50s is common.

**Perimenopause** is the period of years leading up to that point. Hormone levels rise and fall unevenly, so the period may be irregular, heavier, lighter, more frequent or more spaced out. Many of the changes associated with menopause, such as hot flashes, night sweats, sleep changes and mood changes, often begin already at this stage, while the period still comes. Perimenopause can last a few years or much longer, and looks different for every woman.

**Postmenopause** is the entire period after the 12-month point. Some symptoms ease over time, and others can last years.

Menopause can also occur earlier after surgery to remove the ovaries, certain cancer treatments or other medical conditions. Menopause before age 40 is sometimes called premature ovarian insufficiency, and it is worth talking to a doctor about it.

**How the stage is identified.** For many over age 45, doctors identify perimenopause or menopause from your history and symptoms. Blood tests aren't always needed, because hormone levels change from day to day. They are more likely to be used for a younger woman or when the picture isn't clear.

**What MenoMap does and doesn't do.** MenoMap can't tell you which stage you are in. What it can do is keep an honest record of what you notice: flashes, sleep, mood and treatment, so that you and the doctor can look at the same picture.

backTranslations.162:
In medical language, hot flashes and night sweats are called **vasomotor symptoms**. A hot flash is a sudden feeling of heat, usually in the face, neck and chest, sometimes with redness, sweating, a rapid pulse or chills afterward. A night sweat is the same thing during sleep, and it can be strong enough to wake you or wet the bedding.

These are among the most common changes around menopause. Some people have a few mild flashes, and some have many a day, disrupting work and sleep. In some they pass within a few years, and in others they last much longer.

**What can increase the chance of them.** People often notice patterns related to alcohol, caffeine, spicy food, hot rooms, stress or heavy bedding. These triggers vary greatly from person to person, so tracking your tags can be more useful than a general list.

**There are also other causes.** Redness and sweating can also result from thyroid problems, infections, certain medications, anxiety and other conditions. If your symptoms don't fit the usual pattern, or are accompanied by weight loss, high fever or feeling generally unwell, tell a doctor.

**How to describe them well.** Useful details for the visit:
- Roughly how many per day and how many at night
- How strong they are and how long they last
- What they interrupt: sleep, work, conversations, exercise
- What seems to happen before them
- What you tried, and whether it changed anything

MenoMap's "Flash" button and the option to log after the fact are meant to record exactly this, with little effort.

**Help exists.** There are hormonal and non-hormonal treatment options, and also practical ways to cope. Which of them suit you is a conversation worth having with a doctor.

backTranslations.291:
Hormone therapy (often called HRT or MHT) replaces some of the estrogen the body produces less of around menopause. Leading professional guidelines describe it as an effective treatment for hot flashes and night sweats in many people, and it can help with other symptoms too.

**It comes in different forms:** patches, gels, sprays, tablets, and low-dose vaginal preparations for local symptoms such as dryness. Someone who still has a uterus usually receives progestogen alongside the estrogen, to protect the uterine lining.

**The benefit and risks depend on the person:** age, how much time has passed since periods stopped, personal and family history (for example of breast cancer, blood clots, stroke or heart disease), and the type of treatment and how it is taken. So it's a decision made with a doctor who knows your history, not something an app can decide.

**Frequently asked questions:**
- Is hormone therapy right for me, and why or why not?
- What type and form would you recommend, and why?
- What benefit can be expected, and within what time?
- What are my personal risks, and how do they compare to forgoing treatment?
- What should I watch for, and when should we check this again?

**If you're already taking it,** record it in MenoMap (Me > Medications). MenoMap will show your flashes before and after you started, as a coincidence check and not as proof, so you have something concrete to talk about at the follow-up appointment.

MenoMap never suggests starting, stopping or changing a medication.
backTranslations.292: Hormone therapy is a decision made with a doctor
backTranslations.293:
Hormone therapy isn't right for every woman, and some simply prefer other ways. There are several.

**Prescription options.** A few non-hormonal medications have evidence for reducing hot flashes. Among them are certain medications originally developed for other conditions, and a newer group of medications designed specifically for hot flashes. Each has its own benefits, side effects and interactions, so a doctor can help you weigh between them.

**Talk therapy and mind-body approaches.** Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) adapted for menopause has evidence that it makes hot flashes and night sweats less bothersome and improves sleep. Clinical hypnosis has also been studied.

**Practical changes people find helpful:**
- Layers of clothing that can be removed quickly
- A fan by the desk and by the bed
- A cooler bedroom and breathable bedding
- Identifying and reducing personal triggers (MenoMap's tags and experiments help with this)
- Regular exercise and a consistent sleep routine

**Supplements and herbal preparations.** For many of them the evidence is mixed or limited, quality varies, and some interact with other medications. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about everything you take, including over-the-counter products.

**Try one change at a time.** MenoMap's two-week experiments compare your records before a change and during it, and that is easier to judge than a feeling.

backTranslations.416:
Most appointments are short, and it's hard to remember a whole month of nights on the spot. People tend to remember the last days or the worst ones. Simple logging fills the gap.

**What a log gives your doctor:**
- How often the symptoms occur and how strong they are, not just that they occur
- Whether things are improving, worsening or staying the same
- What happened around them: sleep, alcohol, stress, medications
- A starting point for comparison if you try a treatment

**Keep it light.** A log only helps if you keep it up. MenoMap is built around a one-tap "Flash" button and an evening check-in of four questions, so it takes seconds, not a whole notebook.

**Two weeks is a good start.** Two to four weeks of records usually show a clearer picture than one bad week.

**Bring your questions too.** Write what matters most to you: the symptom that bothers you most, what you want to try or avoid, and anything that worries you. MenoMap's Visit tab helps you choose questions and prints them together with your summary.

backTranslations.479:
After 12 months have passed without a period, **any bleeding from the vagina should be checked by a doctor**, even if it happened only once, and even if it was only spotting or a light pink or brown discharge.

In most cases the cause turns out not to be serious. For example, thinning of the vaginal lining or the uterine lining is common. But bleeding after periods have stopped can sometimes be an early sign of a condition that is much easier to treat when found early. So health authorities' guidelines say to check it and not wait.

**If you take hormone therapy,** certain expected bleeding patterns may occur, depending on the type of treatment. Even bleeding that isn't expected on your treatment, is heavier than usual or appears at the wrong time should be checked.

**What to do:**
- Contact your doctor or your health fund, and say you had bleeding after your periods stopped.
- Note the date, the amount and anything else you noticed. MenoMap can save this for you (Me > Cycle).

MenoMap can't tell you why there was bleeding. It will remind you to go for a check and will include it in the visit summary.

backTranslations.529:
Poor sleep is one of the most common complaints in midlife, and it rarely has a single cause.

**Night sweats** can wake you directly, or leave you too warm or damp to fall back asleep.

**Other common factors:**
- Needing to urinate at night
- Anxiety or racing thoughts
- Alcohol, which can help you fall asleep but tends to interrupt sleep in the second half of the night
- Caffeine late in the day
- Pain, restless legs or a partner's snoring
- Snoring or pauses in breathing, which can be a sign of sleep apnea (worth raising, especially if you are very sleepy during the day)

**What tends to help.** A cool, dark room; breathable bedding and layers that are easy to remove; a consistent wake-up time; and less alcohol close to bedtime. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a well-studied structured approach, and many doctors can refer to it.

**What to log.** For a week or two, note your sleep score, night flashes, alcohol and late caffeine. Tonight's check-in and MenoMap's flash log do this in a few taps. If you use an Apple Watch, MenoMap can show your sleep and wrist temperature from Health alongside night sweats, as context and not as explanation.

**When to get checked.** Talk to a doctor if the poor sleep affects your safety (for example while driving), your mood or daily life, or if you notice pauses in breathing or gasping at night.

162.to:
בשפה הרפואית, גלי חום והזעות לילה נקראים **תסמינים וזומוטוריים**. גל חום הוא תחושה פתאומית של חום, לרוב בפנים, בצוואר ובחזה, לפעמים עם אדמומיות, הזעה, דופק מהיר או צמרמורת אחר כך. הזעת לילה היא אותה תופעה בזמן השינה, והיא יכולה להיות חזקה מספיק כדי להעיר אותך או להרטיב את המצעים.

אלה מהשינויים הנפוצים ביותר סביב גיל המעבר. יש מי שחווה כמה גלים קלים, ויש מי שחווה גלים רבים ביום, שמשבשים את העבודה ואת השינה. אצל חלק הם חולפים תוך כמה שנים, ואצל אחרים הם נמשכים הרבה יותר זמן.

**מה יכול להגביר את הסיכוי להם.** אנשים מבחינים לעיתים קרובות בדפוסים הקשורים לאלכוהול, קפאין, אוכל חריף, חדרים חמים, לחץ או מצעים כבדים. הגורמים האלה משתנים מאוד מאדם לאדם, ולכן מעקב אחר התגיות שלך יכול להיות שימושי יותר מרשימה כללית.

**יש גם סיבות אחרות.** אדמומיות והזעה יכולות לנבוע גם מבעיות בבלוטת התריס, זיהומים, תרופות מסוימות, חרדה ומצבים אחרים. אם התסמינים שלך לא מתאימים לדפוס הרגיל, או מלווים בירידה במשקל, חום או הרגשה כללית לא טובה, ספרי על כך לרופא/ה.

**איך לתאר אותם היטב.** פרטים שימושיים לביקור:
- בערך כמה ביום וכמה בלילה
- כמה הם חזקים ולכמה זמן הם נמשכים
- מה הם קוטעים: שינה, עבודה, שיחות, פעילות גופנית
- מה נראה שקורה לפניהם
- מה ניסית, והאם זה שינה משהו

כפתור ״גל״ של MenoMap והאפשרות לרשום בדיעבד נועדו לתעד בדיוק את זה, בלי הרבה מאמץ.

**יש עזרה.** יש אפשרויות טיפול הורמונליות ולא הורמונליות, וגם דרכים מעשיות להתמודד. אילו מהן מתאימות לך – זו שיחה שכדאי לנהל עם רופא/ה.
